meta.name: Azure Network Engineer Associate (AZ-700)
meta.notes: Initial pack — 12 questions across the AZ-700 exam domains: hybrid connectivity, core networking, routing, network security, private access, and load balancing. keyword-balance pass. v1.1: +10 — ASGs, NAT gateway SNAT, ExpressRoute peerings, P2S VPN, service vs private endpoints, Bastion, DNS Private Resolver, Traffic Analytics, Front Door, DDoS Network Protection. [scheduled-agent hardening pass 2026-08-24: full-pack rewrite of all 22 questions — rebalanced positions to A/B/C/D = 5/6/6/5, no run > 2, removed self-defeating distractor clauses (embedded 'but it does...' explanations) on Q2/Q5/Q6/Q8/Q9/Q17, removed reverse length-tell on the correct answer, ensured each explanation addresses every distractor]

questions.question: You need a site-to-site VPN connection into an Azure virtual network that survives the failure of a single Azure VPN gateway instance and also provides higher aggregate throughput. Which configuration should you use?
options: Deploy the VPN gateway in active-active mode, which provisions two gateway instances each with its own public IP address
Deploy a single Basic SKU VPN gateway and rely on the Azure platform SLA to recover the instance after a failure
Create two separate VPN gateways in the GatewaySubnet of the same virtual network for redundancy
Provision a route-based gateway in active-passive mode and add a second local network gateway on premises
questions.explanation: Active-active mode provisions two gateway instances, each with its own public IP, so the on-premises device builds tunnels to both — surviving a single-instance failure and increasing aggregate throughput. The Basic SKU is a single instance and supports neither active-active nor BGP, so it cannot meet the requirement. A virtual network supports at most one VPN gateway, so 'two gateways in one GatewaySubnet' is not a valid deployment. A second local network gateway simply represents another on-premises site, and active-passive keeps only one Azure instance forwarding traffic at a time — no throughput gain and no dual-instance HA.

questions.question: A company connects to Microsoft over an ExpressRoute circuit and must reach both Azure IaaS VMs inside virtual networks and Microsoft 365 plus public Azure PaaS endpoints over that same circuit. Which peering configuration is required?
options: Azure private peering only, since it carries all Microsoft traffic once the circuit is provisioned
Microsoft peering only, since it supersedes and replaces private peering on modern circuits
Azure private peering for the virtual networks and Microsoft peering for Microsoft 365 and public PaaS services
Azure public peering for every destination, since it was renamed to Microsoft peering with no functional change
questions.explanation: An ExpressRoute circuit exposes two routing domains: private peering carries traffic to virtual networks (IaaS), and Microsoft peering carries traffic to Microsoft public services such as Microsoft 365 and public Azure PaaS endpoints. Both destinations require both peerings enabled on the circuit. Private peering alone cannot reach Microsoft 365 or public PaaS endpoints. Microsoft peering does not replace private peering — VNet traffic still requires private peering. Azure public peering is a deprecated legacy peering type; Microsoft peering added scoping via route filters and is not a rename of it.

questions.question: An organization has 30 branch offices and workloads in 6 Azure regions. It wants a Microsoft-managed hub-and-spoke topology where branches connect with site-to-site VPN and SD-WAN, and routing between hubs and spokes is handled automatically. Which Azure offering should it adopt?
options: Azure Virtual WAN with a virtual hub in each region
A self-managed hub virtual network in each region, peered together in a manually maintained mesh
An Azure Route Server deployed in every spoke virtual network to exchange BGP routes with the branches
A dedicated Azure VPN gateway deployed in every spoke virtual network to terminate branch tunnels
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual WAN provides Microsoft-managed virtual hubs that aggregate site-to-site VPN, point-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute, and SD-WAN connectivity, with automatic any-to-any routing between hubs and spokes — the design the scenario asks for. A manually meshed hub-and-spoke topology is exactly the operational burden Virtual WAN removes and does not offer managed SD-WAN integration. Azure Route Server exchanges BGP routes with a network virtual appliance inside a VNet; it does not build a managed multi-region hub topology. A VPN gateway per spoke means 30 branches × 6 regions of separate tunnels with no shared routing plane, which does not scale.

questions.question: A hub virtual network contains an Azure VPN gateway. Spoke virtual networks are peered to the hub and must reach on-premises networks through that single gateway without each spoke having its own gateway. Which peering settings achieve this?
options: Enable 'Allow gateway transit' on both sides of every hub-to-spoke peering to permit bidirectional gateway use
On the hub side of the peering enable 'Allow gateway transit', and on the spoke side enable 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway'
On the hub side enable 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway', and on the spoke side enable 'Allow gateway transit'
Deploy a VPN gateway in every spoke and disable gateway transit on all hub-to-spoke peerings
questions.explanation: The VNet that owns the gateway (the hub) must set 'Allow gateway transit' on its side of the peering, and the VNet that consumes it (each spoke) must set 'Use the remote virtual network's gateway' on its side — exactly this asymmetric pair. Enabling transit on both sides does nothing useful because neither side is the consumer, and only one gateway can be transited at a time. Reversing the two flags (transit on the spoke, use-remote-gateway on the hub) advertises the spoke as the gateway provider, which is backward. Placing a gateway in every spoke defeats the centralized hub-and-spoke design and incurs a gateway cost per spoke.

questions.question: VMs spread across several spoke virtual networks must resolve each other by hostname automatically as the VMs are created and deleted, with no manual record maintenance. What should you configure?
options: A public Azure DNS zone containing one manually created A record per VM in every spoke
A custom DNS server VM in the hub running BIND with zone transfers to each spoke's own BIND replica
Only the Azure-provided default DNS resolver at 168.63.129.16 with no additional configuration
An Azure Private DNS zone linked to each virtual network with auto-registration enabled on those links
questions.explanation: An Azure Private DNS zone linked to the virtual networks with the auto-registration option creates and removes DNS records automatically as VMs are provisioned and deprovisioned, and it resolves those names across all linked VNets — exactly the requirement. A public DNS zone needs manual record maintenance and exposes internal hostnames on the internet. Running BIND with zone transfers reproduces the manual-maintenance problem the requirement rules out and adds a VM to operate. The default Azure-provided resolver (168.63.129.16) only resolves hostnames within a single virtual network, not across peered spokes.

questions.question: All traffic between two spoke virtual networks must be inspected by a network virtual appliance (NVA) located in the hub virtual network. What is the correct way to force spoke-to-spoke traffic through the NVA?
options: Apply a network security group on each spoke subnet that permits only the NVA's IP address as a source and destination
Enable 'Allow forwarded traffic' on the spoke-to-spoke virtual network peering between the two spokes
Configure BGP on the NVA and rely on Azure system routes to redirect spoke-to-spoke traffic automatically
Associate a user-defined route table on each spoke subnet with a route to the other spoke's prefix using next hop type 'Virtual appliance' set to the NVA's private IP address
questions.explanation: A user-defined route on each spoke subnet, targeting the other spoke's address prefix with next hop type 'Virtual appliance' pointing at the NVA's private IP, is the mechanism that steers that traffic through the NVA for inspection. NSGs enforce allow/deny decisions on the packet's path but do not change routing, so they cannot redirect flows. 'Allow forwarded traffic' permits transit packets on a peering but does not itself steer traffic anywhere. BGP into the NVA needs an Azure Route Server to be redistributed into subnets; system routes alone send spoke-to-spoke traffic directly between the peered VNets without visiting the hub.

questions.question: A security team needs centralized, stateful filtering of outbound traffic by fully qualified domain name (FQDN), threat intelligence-based filtering, and centralized logging for an entire hub-and-spoke network. Which service meets these requirements?
options: Network security groups applied to every subnet in the topology and referenced from a central policy document
Application security groups referenced inside network security group rules for each application tier
Azure Firewall deployed in the hub virtual network as the egress inspection point
Azure DDoS Protection enabled on the hub virtual network and its public IP addresses
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful cloud-native network firewall that supports application rules with FQDN filtering, threat intelligence-based filtering, and centralized logging to Azure Monitor — the exact combination the scenario requires. Network security groups filter by IP address, port, protocol, and service tags but cannot match arbitrary FQDNs or apply threat intelligence. Application security groups only group NICs so NSG rules can reference them; they add no new filtering capabilities. Azure DDoS Protection mitigates volumetric attacks against public IPs and performs no application-layer egress filtering at all.

questions.question: You must make an Azure SQL Database reachable from a virtual network using a private IP address inside that VNet, with no exposure of the database on the public internet. Which feature should you use?
options: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql configured on the subnet, so the database's public IP is reached over the Azure backbone
A private endpoint for the SQL Database that projects a private IP address from the subnet onto the database
The database's public endpoint restricted by the logical SQL server firewall to the VNet's outbound public IP
An ExpressRoute Microsoft peering advertised toward the SQL Database's public service prefix
questions.explanation: A private endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP address from the subnet that maps to the PaaS resource, so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone and the service needs no public exposure. A service endpoint still targets the service's public IP — it optimizes the path and identifies the subnet to the service's firewall, but the public endpoint remains reachable. A firewall-restricted public endpoint is still a public endpoint on the internet. ExpressRoute Microsoft peering provides reachability to public Microsoft services over a private circuit but does not project a private IP into a VNet, so the database still has no VNet-local private address.

questions.question: A backend pool of VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer must be resilient to the loss of an availability zone, and the VMs need a defined, explicit outbound internet connection. Which design is correct?
options: A Basic SKU public Load Balancer relying on default outbound access provided by the platform
An internal Standard SKU Load Balancer, because internal load balancers also provide outbound internet access to their backend pool
A Standard SKU public Load Balancer paired with an outbound rule, or an attached NAT gateway, for explicit egress
A Basic SKU internal Load Balancer combined with instance-level public IP addresses on each VM
questions.explanation: The Standard SKU Load Balancer is zone-aware and zone-redundant, and pairing it with an explicit outbound rule — or, preferably, a NAT gateway — provides deterministic SNAT egress for its backend pool. The Basic SKU is not zone-redundant, is being retired, and depends on implicit default outbound access that Microsoft is removing. An internal Load Balancer has no public frontend and therefore never provides outbound internet connectivity. A Basic internal Load Balancer paired with per-VM public IPs still fails the zone-resilience requirement and exposes every VM directly to the internet.

questions.question: A web application needs Layer 7 load balancing with URL path-based routing (for example, /images and /api directed to different backend pools), TLS termination, and protection against common web exploits such as SQL injection. Which Azure service should you choose?
options: Azure Load Balancer with health probes on each backend pool and hash-based session affinity
Azure Application Gateway on the Web Application Firewall (WAF) tier
Azure Traffic Manager configured with weighted routing to backend pools in each region
Azure Front Door deployed without the Web Application Firewall enabled
questions.explanation: Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer that provides URL path-based routing, multi-site hosting, and TLS termination, and its WAF tier protects against OWASP Top 10 exploits such as SQL injection — every requirement in one service. Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and cannot inspect or route by URL path. Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing with no path awareness, no TLS termination, and no web application firewall. Front Door without WAF satisfies the routing and TLS needs but leaves the application unprotected against exactly the web exploits called out.

questions.question: A global application is deployed across four Azure regions. You need to route each user to the lowest-latency healthy region, terminate TLS and cache static content at the network edge, and fail over automatically. Which service best meets all of these needs?
options: Azure Front Door
Azure Traffic Manager using the performance routing method against endpoints in each region
An internal Standard SKU Load Balancer spanning all four regions as a cross-region frontend
Azure DNS configured with weighted A-record sets pointing at each region's public IP
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global, edge-based Layer 7 entry point that performs latency-based routing to the closest healthy backend, terminates TLS at the edge, caches static content with its built-in content delivery capability, and fails over automatically without waiting on DNS TTLs. Traffic Manager is DNS-only: it can do performance routing and health-based failover but cannot terminate TLS or cache content, and its failover speed is bounded by the client's DNS TTL. A Load Balancer is regional, and internal load balancers have no internet-facing role at all. Weighted DNS records provide neither latency-based routing, TLS offload, nor edge caching.

questions.question: Operators report intermittent connectivity from a VM to an external endpoint. They need continuous, alertable monitoring of latency, packet loss, and reachability over time between the VM and that endpoint. Which Azure Network Watcher capability should you use?
options: IP flow verify against the source VM's NIC and the destination address and port
Next hop lookup from the source VM toward the destination endpoint
Effective security rules view exported for the source VM's network interface
Connection monitor between the source VM and the external endpoint
questions.explanation: Connection monitor provides continuous, ongoing monitoring of reachability, latency, and packet loss between a source such as a VM and a destination, recording metrics over time in Azure Monitor and supporting alerts — the exact operational need. IP flow verify is a one-time check of whether a specific packet is permitted by the effective NSG rules. Next hop returns the routing decision for a single packet at the moment it is asked. Effective security rules shows the aggregated NSG rules currently applied to a network interface. All three of the alternatives are point-in-time diagnostics rather than continuous monitoring.

questions.question: NSG rules reference dozens of individual VM IP addresses for the web, app and database tiers, and every scale-out means editing rules. How do you simplify this while keeping tier-to-tier restrictions?
options: Assign static private IPs from reserved ranges per tier and reference those CIDR ranges in the NSG rules
Application security groups: tag each NIC with its tier's ASG and write NSG rules between ASGs
Replace the NSG with an Azure Firewall policy that uses FQDN rules for each tier's VM hostnames
Move each tier into its own dedicated virtual network connected through global VNet peering
questions.explanation: Application security groups make NSG rules membership-based: NICs join the web/app/db ASG, rules say 'allow app-asg → db-asg:1433', and new instances inherit the rules simply by joining the group — no rule edits at scale-out. Reserved IP ranges still demand manual IP discipline and per-tier subnet planning, and drift as scale grows. Azure Firewall FQDN rules target outbound name-based traffic to the internet, not internal east-west VM-to-VM tiering. Dedicated per-tier VNets connected by peering solves a topology problem, not a rule-sprawl problem, and multiplies peering and routing complexity.

questions.question: VMs in a subnet make thousands of short outbound connections to the same external service and start failing intermittently with SNAT port exhaustion behind a public load balancer. What is the recommended fix?
options: Enable TCP reset on idle timeout on the load balancer so exhausted flows recycle faster under load
Add a second public IP to each VM's NIC so half of the flows originate from a different source address
Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet so outbound flows use its scalable SNAT port pool
Lower the load balancer health probe interval so unhealthy ports are reclaimed more quickly
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway is Azure's recommended outbound path: it provides up to 64k SNAT ports per attached public IP (scalable to 16 IPs), dynamic allocation, and takes precedence over load-balancer outbound SNAT for the subnet — the direct fix for port exhaustion. TCP reset on idle timeout speeds up idle-flow cleanup but does not add ports, so it only postpones the problem. Adding public IPs to each VM removes SNAT for those VMs but exposes every VM directly to the internet, which is a security trade-off, not a scaling fix. Probe interval tuning affects health decisions, not SNAT port allocation at all.

questions.question: An ExpressRoute circuit must carry traffic to the company's own VNets AND to Microsoft 365 endpoints. Which peering configuration is correct?
options: Public peering for the VNets and private peering for Microsoft 365, with route filters applied on both paths
Private peering alone, since Microsoft 365 endpoints resolve to private addresses over ExpressRoute
Two separate ExpressRoute circuits, because one circuit supports only one peering type at a time
Private peering for the VNets and Microsoft peering (with route filters) for Microsoft 365
questions.explanation: Private peering extends your network to your VNets; Microsoft peering carries traffic to Microsoft public services such as Microsoft 365 and public Azure PaaS endpoints, with route filters selecting which service prefixes are advertised to your edge. One ExpressRoute circuit supports both peerings simultaneously — a second circuit is not needed. 'Azure public peering' is a retired peering type and is not the same as Microsoft peering. Microsoft 365 endpoints remain public IP addresses even when reached over ExpressRoute, so private peering alone cannot route to them.

questions.question: Fifteen developers working from home need individual encrypted access to VMs in a VNet, authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID, without installing a branch VPN device anywhere. What do you deploy?
options: A site-to-site VPN from each developer's home router to the VNet's gateway subnet
Point-to-site VPN on the virtual network gateway with Microsoft Entra ID authentication
ExpressRoute Direct with a partner exchange port reserved for the development team
VNet service endpoints configured for the Microsoft.Compute resource provider on each subnet
questions.explanation: Point-to-site VPN is per-device: each developer runs the Azure VPN Client, authenticates with Entra ID, and gets an encrypted tunnel into the VNet — no on-premises VPN hardware required. Site-to-site VPN assumes a VPN device at each site (15 home routers with static configuration is the wrong model). ExpressRoute Direct is dedicated 10/100 Gbps circuit infrastructure for enterprises, dramatically overkill and slow to provision for 15 remote developers. Service endpoints connect a subnet to a PaaS service; they do nothing to give end users encrypted access to VMs.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a service endpoint and a private endpoint for reaching an Azure Storage account from a VNet?
options: Service endpoints require a private DNS zone per service, while private endpoints work with no DNS changes at all
Service endpoints encrypt the storage traffic, while private endpoints rely on the application layer for encryption
Private endpoints are free of charge, while service endpoints are billed per gigabyte of data processed
A service endpoint optimizes the route to the service's PUBLIC endpoint; a private endpoint gives the service a PRIVATE IP inside your VNet
questions.explanation: Service endpoints keep traffic on the Azure backbone toward the service's public IP and identify the source subnet to the service's firewall — the service never enters your VNet address space. A private endpoint injects a NIC with a private IP from your VNet, so the service is reachable over VPN/ExpressRoute and from peered networks (which is precisely why it needs private DNS zones and is billed per hour and per GB). Service endpoints do not add extra encryption over Azure's default in-transit protection. Private endpoints are not free; both features cost, but private endpoints carry hourly plus data-processing charges.

questions.question: Security policy forbids public IP addresses on any IaaS VM, yet administrators need browser-based RDP and SSH to VMs across several VNets. Which service satisfies this?
options: Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud that opens management ports on request for approved source IPs
An internal load balancer with inbound NAT rules mapping high ports to each VM's RDP or SSH port
Azure Bastion (Standard SKU or higher) deployed in a hub VNet and reachable from the spoke VNets
Network security group rules restricting ports 3389 and 22 to the administrators' home IP ranges
questions.explanation: Azure Bastion provides TLS-wrapped RDP/SSH through the portal (or the native client) directly to VMs' private IPs — no public IP is needed on the VMs, and the Standard SKU with IP-based connection reaches VMs in peered VNets from a hub deployment. Just-in-time VM access still presupposes a public path to the VM's management port and only narrows the window during which it is open. An internal load balancer has no public frontend, so administrators cannot reach it from the internet at all. NSG rules pinned to the administrators' home IPs still require public IPs on the VMs, which the policy forbids.

questions.question: On-premises clients must resolve names in an Azure Private DNS zone (privatelink.database.windows.net) to reach private endpoints. Conditional forwarders cannot target the 168.63.129.16 resolver across VPN. What should you deploy?
options: Azure DNS Private Resolver with an inbound endpoint that on-premises DNS servers forward queries to
A secondary copy of the private zone hosted on the on-premises DNS servers with zone transfers configured
Custom DNS settings on every on-premises client pointing directly at the Azure-provided resolver address
A public DNS zone with the same records, so name resolution succeeds from any network location
questions.explanation: DNS Private Resolver's inbound endpoint exposes a routable private IP inside a VNet that on-premises servers can conditionally forward to; the resolver then answers against the private zones linked to that VNet. 168.63.129.16 is link-local to Azure VMs and unreachable over VPN or ExpressRoute, whether forwarded from servers or configured directly on clients. Azure Private DNS zones do not support zone transfers, so no secondary copy can be maintained on premises. Publishing private endpoint IPs in a public zone leaks the internal topology and breaks the privacy model that private endpoints exist to provide.

questions.question: The security team asks which on-premises subnets have been connecting to which Azure VMs over the past month, with traffic volumes, visualized geographically. Which capability answers this?
options: Connection troubleshoot in Network Watcher run against each VM pair the team cares about
Effective security rules view exported weekly for every network interface in the subscription
NSG flow logs analyzed with Traffic Analytics in Log Analytics
Azure Monitor metrics on each NIC summed across the month with a workbook visualization
questions.explanation: NSG flow logs record allowed and denied flows per rule (source, destination, port, byte counts), and Traffic Analytics aggregates them in Log Analytics into traffic patterns, talking-pairs, and geo-mapped visualizations over time — exactly the retrospective question asked. Connection troubleshoot performs on-demand end-to-end checks between two endpoints, not historical aggregation. Effective security rules shows the current NSG rule set on a NIC, not who actually talked to whom. NIC-level Azure Monitor metrics report byte counters, which give no flow-level source/destination detail and cannot be mapped geographically.

questions.question: A global HTTP application needs TLS termination at Microsoft's edge, anycast-based instant failover between regional backends, URL-path routing, and an integrated WAF. Which service is designed for this combination?
options: Azure Front Door (Standard/Premium)
Traffic Manager with performance routing fronting regional application gateways in each geography
A cross-region load balancer distributing layer-4 flows to regional public load balancers in each region
Application Gateway v2 instances deployed per region behind a round-robin DNS record set
questions.explanation: Front Door is Microsoft's global Layer 7 entry point: anycast edge POPs terminate TLS close to users, route on URL paths and headers, fail over almost instantly without waiting on DNS TTLs, and the Premium SKU integrates a WAF — every requirement in one service. Traffic Manager is DNS-based, so failover speed is bounded by the client TTL, and it cannot terminate TLS or route paths. Cross-region Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and offers no TLS termination, path routing, or WAF. Per-region Application Gateways behind DNS round-robin reinvent Traffic Manager poorly and still lack anycast-based instant failover.

questions.question: After a volumetric attack against a public-facing workload, the business wants tuned, telemetry-backed DDoS mitigation on its public IPs, cost protection guarantees, and access to a rapid-response team. What do you enable?
options: The default infrastructure-level DDoS protection that Azure applies to every public IP for free
Azure DDoS Network Protection on the virtual network hosting the public IP addresses
A WAF policy in prevention mode attached to the application gateway fronting the workload
Azure Firewall Premium with IDPS signatures set to alert-and-deny for inbound traffic flows
questions.explanation: Azure DDoS Network Protection (the paid tier) adds adaptive, per-resource tuned mitigation, attack analytics and telemetry, access to the DDoS Rapid Response team, and cost-protection credits for scale-out during attacks — every specific ask in the scenario. The free infrastructure DDoS protection is untuned to the workload, produces no per-resource telemetry, and offers no rapid-response team or cost-protection guarantees. A WAF stops Layer 7 application attacks such as SQL injection but does not absorb volumetric floods. Azure Firewall Premium's IDPS inspects permitted flows for signatures rather than mitigating volumetric attacks.
